instructions: Put 12 oz of the rice cakes in a bowl, cover them with cold water and leave them to soak for 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, rinse the 1.5 cups rice in a few changes of water until the water runs mostly clear. Cook it in a rice cooker, or in a covered pot with 1 3/4 cups water over low heat for 18 minutes, then leave it covered off the heat for 10 minutes.

In a large bowl, stir together 3 tbsp gochujang, 1 tbsp of the gochugaru, 3 tbsp soy sauce, 3 tbsp mirin, 1 1/2 tbsp sugar, the 1 1/2 tsp curry powder and the 1 1/2 tbsp sesame oil. Mince the 4 garlic cloves and peel and grate 1 tsp of the ginger into the bowl, then stir again.
Cut the 1.5 lbs chicken thighs into 1 1/2 inch pieces. Add them to the sauce and stir until every piece is coated. Leave them in the sauce while you cut the vegetables.
Cut half the cabbage into 1 1/2 inch pieces. Peel the sweet potato, cut it in half lengthwise and slice it 1/4 inch thick. Cut 3 of the scallions into 2 inch lengths.
Stack 8 of the perilla leaves, roll them up and slice them into wide strips. If you can't find perilla leaves, leave them out.
Put the last 1 tsp gochugaru in a small bowl for the table.

Heat the 1 tbsp vegetable oil in your largest skillet or a wok over medium high. Add the chicken with all its sauce, the cabbage, the sweet potato and the drained rice cakes. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring and turning everything often so the sauce doesn't scorch. If it starts to stick, add 1/4 cup water and turn the heat down a little.

Add the scallions and perilla leaves and keep stirring for 3 to 4 minutes, until the sweet potato and rice cakes are soft when you bite one. You're cooking the chicken to 175°F, so if you have a thermometer, check the thickest piece. No thermometer? Cut a piece open. It's done when there's no pink left.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Sprinkle the 1 tbsp sesame seeds over the top.
Serve with the rice, with the gochugaru on the side.
method_notes: Both read versions coat boneless chicken thighs in a gochujang, gochugaru, soy, rice wine, sugar, garlic and curry powder sauce and cook it in one wide pan with cabbage, sweet potato, rice cakes and perilla leaves. Korean Bapsang lets the chicken sit in the sauce while the vegetables are cut and puts everything in the pan at once, adding a splash of water if it sticks, and Beyond Kimchee sets the pan up cold and adds half the perilla at the start. Both finish the leftover sauce in the pan with rice and seaweed as fried rice. This one follows Korean Bapsang scaled to 1.5 lbs chicken, keeps the chili flakes in the pot to a mild amount with the rest at the table, and serves it with steamed rice.
